lessons.t: Error analysis first: read 100 real outputs before writing a metric
lessons.html:
The most common eval mistake is starting with metrics. A team adopts off-the-shelf scores for helpfulness, coherence and toxicity, builds a dashboard, and watches numbers that never move with the complaints users actually make. Generic metrics measure what is easy to define. Your feature fails in specific ways that only reading reveals.

Error analysis is the discipline of reading real outputs, naming what went wrong and counting it. Practitioners such as Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, who teach it widely, describe a method borrowed from qualitative research.

  1. Sample traces. Pull about 100 recent production traces, including the full context, tool calls and output. Mix a random sample with traces flagged by users or by signals such as retries and escalations.
  2. Open coding. Read each trace and write a short free-form note on the first thing that went wrong. Don’t use a predefined list. A note reads like “quoted the 2024 refund window” or “asked for an order number the user already gave”.
  3. Axial coding. Group the notes into a small taxonomy of failure modes and count each one.
  4. Stop at saturation. Keep reading until new traces stop producing new categories. For a new feature that is often 100 traces or more.
Failure mode (illustrative)Count in 100 tracesSeverityPriority
Cites a superseded policy version14High: wrong money outcome1
Asks for information already given11Medium: friction3
Answers when it should hand off to a human6High: compliance2
Overlong answer, key step buried9Low4
Tool called with wrong date format4Medium: silent failure5

The taxonomy is the output that matters. Each row becomes a candidate eval criterion (Lesson 2), a candidate fix (Chapter 4’s context levers), and a line on the roadmap (Lesson 6). Priority comes from frequency times severity, so a rare failure with a legal consequence can outrank a frequent cosmetic one.

Who does the reading

The PM or a named domain expert, not a contractor and not a model. Husain and Shankar’s evals FAQ recommends one person with domain authority as the final judge of quality, and advises annotating at least 30 traces yourself before letting an AI assistant propose categories, so its suggestions don’t anchor yours. Reading is also how the team learns what the product does in the wild, which no dashboard teaches.

Shankar and colleagues found in a 2024 study that people’s evaluation criteria shift as they grade outputs. They call this criteria drift. You can’t write a complete rubric before you see outputs, because seeing outputs is how you discover what you care about. Plan for the rubric to change during the first two or three rounds of reading, and version it.

Repeat error analysis after every significant change, on a regular cadence for live features, and whenever online metrics move without an obvious cause. A typical rhythm is 30 to 50 traces a week once the taxonomy is stable.

What changes for you

  • Block your calendar for the first round of reading: about 100 traces, two to three hours, before any metric is agreed.
  • Ask for the failure taxonomy with counts in every quality review, and treat a dashboard without one as unfinished.
  • Name one quality owner with authority to rule on borderline cases.

lessons.t: Golden sets, rubrics and coverage of the long tail
lessons.html:
A golden set is a versioned collection of inputs with either reference outputs or grading criteria. It turns “good” into something a machine can check on every change. Building one well means making three decisions: where the cases come from, how they are graded, and how big the set needs to be.

Where cases come from

SourceWhat it gives youWatch out for
Random production samplesThe real distribution of requestsUnderweights rare, high-stakes cases
Failure taxonomy (Lesson 1)Targeted tests for known problemsOverfitting the set to last month’s bugs
Support tickets and escalationsCases users cared enough to reportSelection bias toward vocal users
Adversarial and edge casesInjection attempts, empty input, mixed languages, contradictionsSpending the whole set on the exotic
Synthetic casesCoverage of combinations you lack data forRepetitive phrasing; poor estimate of real failure rates

For synthetic cases, define dimensions first (for example, issue type × customer mood × account state), write a few combinations by hand, then generate more. Asking a model for “test questions” produces bland, similar queries. Compare synthetic cases against real ones as soon as you have traffic.

Rubrics

Grade with several specific binary criteria rather than one 1–5 score. A 1–5 scale gets applied inconsistently between graders, invites the middle value and needs larger samples to show a difference. “Cites the current refund window: pass or fail” is unambiguous. Report a pass-all rate (all criteria pass) and per-criterion rates for diagnosis. Mark a few criteria as critical, so any failure on them fails the case and can block a release.

Prefer the cheapest reliable grader for each criterion: code (exact match, regex, schema validation, unit tests, a database lookup), then an LLM judge (Lesson 3), then a person. Anthropic’s guidance on agent evals makes the same recommendation and adds one: read the transcripts behind failures to confirm the grader didn’t reject a valid answer.

How many cases

Start with 20 to 50. Early on, changes have large effects and a small set detects them. But know what a small set can’t tell you. With 50 cases and an 80% pass rate, the 95% confidence interval is roughly ±11 points; at 50% it is about ±14. A move from 78% to 82% on 50 cases is noise. To detect smaller changes, grow the set toward a few hundred, run each case several times, and compare variants case by case on the same inputs.

Keep the set honest

Never copy eval cases into few-shot examples or the system prompt. Keep a held-out slice nobody tunes against. Version the set and the rubric together, and record which version produced each score, or trends become meaningless.

What changes for you

  • Write acceptance criteria as binary rubric items with named graders, and mark the critical ones.
  • Require a coverage matrix showing slices (user type, language, request type, risk level) and case counts per slice.
  • Read every reported score with its sample size and interval. Small differences on small sets are not evidence.

lessons.t: LLM-as-judge: when it works and how to calibrate it
lessons.html:
An LLM judge is a model prompted to grade an output against a criterion. It makes rubric grading cheap enough to run on every change and on samples of live traffic. It is also a second probabilistic system that can be wrong in systematic ways, so a judge is a measurement instrument that needs calibrating before you trust its readings.

Known biases

Zheng et al.’s 2023 paper Judging LLM-as-a-Judge found that strong judges agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time on their benchmarks, about the level at which humans agree with each other. It also documented three biases that still show up in practice:

  • Position bias. In pairwise comparisons the verdict depends on which answer is shown first. Run both orders and count only consistent verdicts.
  • Verbosity bias. Longer answers get rated higher. Put length expectations in the criterion, or check length with code.
  • Self-enhancement bias. Judges can favour outputs like their own. Use a judge from a different model family where you can.
Judges work wellJudges struggle
One narrow, binary criterion per judge“Rate overall quality 1–10”
A reference answer or source text to compare againstExpert domain correctness with no reference (legal, clinical, tax)
Clear pass and fail examples in the judge promptLong, multi-step agent transcripts graded in one pass
Style, tone, format, groundedness in supplied sourcesFacts the judge itself doesn’t know

Calibrating against humans

Build one judge per failure mode. Have your quality owner label a balanced set, roughly 100 to 200 examples with a meaningful number of both passes and fails. Split it: a small slice for examples inside the judge prompt, a development slice for iterating on the prompt, and a held-out test slice used once at the end. Then measure two numbers on the test slice, not overall accuracy:

  • Sensitivity on passes: of outputs a human passed, the share the judge passed.
  • Specificity on fails: of outputs a human failed, the share the judge failed.

Accuracy alone hides the failure that matters. If 90% of outputs pass, a judge that passes everything scores 90% accuracy and catches nothing.

Correcting a judged pass rate

If the judge passes true passes at rate s and wrongly passes true fails at rate f, the observed pass rate p relates to the true rate θ by p = θs + (1 − θ)f, so θ = (p − f) / (s − f). Illustrative numbers: s = 0.95, f = 0.10, observed p = 0.80 gives θ ≈ 0.82. When f is large, a judged score near your threshold doesn’t tell you which side of it you are on.

Pin the judge’s model version and prompt like production code. Re-calibrate whenever either changes, when the rubric changes, and on a regular schedule (monthly is common), by having a person grade a fresh sample of 30 to 50 judged cases and checking agreement. A drift in agreement is an incident for your measurement system.

What changes for you

  • Ask for each judge’s sensitivity and specificity against human labels, with the sample size. Don’t accept “the judge agrees with us” without numbers.
  • Require one judge per criterion, a pinned judge model, and a re-calibration date in the eval spec.
  • Use code graders wherever a rule can decide, and keep human grading on the criteria where judges are weakest.

lessons.t: Offline evals, online metrics and the gap between them
lessons.html:
Offline evals run a fixed dataset against a candidate system before release. Online metrics measure what happens with real users after release. You need both, because each is blind where the other sees.

Offline evalOnline metrics
AnswersDid this change make the system better on cases we chose?Are users getting value, and is anything breaking?
WhenBefore merge and releaseAfter release, continuously
SpeedMinutes to hoursDays to weeks for significance
StrengthControlled, repeatable, case-by-case comparisonThe real distribution, real stakes, real behaviour
Blind spotRequests you didn’t think to includeWhy something happened; rare high-severity failures

Online signals for AI features

Explicit feedback (thumbs up or down) is sparse and skewed toward strong reactions. Behavioural signals are usually more informative:

  • Acceptance: suggestion inserted, draft sent, action approved.
  • Edit distance: how much users change a draft before using it.
  • Retry and regenerate rate: the clearest sign the first answer missed.
  • Escalation and abandonment: handoffs to a human, sessions that end without the task done.
  • Downstream outcome: ticket resolved without reopening, code merged and not reverted.
  • Online judges: your calibrated judges run on a sample of live traffic, which gives rubric scores on the real distribution.

Pair each primary metric with guardrail metrics that must not get worse, such as cost per session, latency, escalation rate and policy violations.

Why offline and online disagree

Offline scores go up and user metrics stay flat more often than teams expect. The usual causes are distribution shift (the golden set reflects last quarter’s users), saturation (the set is too easy to separate good from great), grading what is easy rather than what matters, and users adapting to the product in ways the set doesn’t represent. Goodhart’s law applies with force: once the team tunes against the golden set, it measures less of what you care about.

When they disagree, trust production and fix the eval

Pull the traces behind the online movement, run error analysis on them, and add the new failure modes to the golden set. The offline eval is a model of production, and it is the one that needs updating.

Close the loop on a schedule. Each week, sample fresh production traces into a review queue and promote the instructive ones into the golden set. Each release, plot offline score change against online metric change. Over several releases this tells you whether your offline eval predicts anything. If it doesn’t, it isn’t ready to gate releases.

What changes for you

  • Define one primary online metric and two or three guardrails per AI feature, and instrument them before launch.
  • Track whether offline gains predicted online gains across the last several releases, and say so in quality reviews.
  • Make promoting production traces into the golden set a weekly task with an owner.

lessons.t: Regression gates for prompt, model and tool changes
lessons.html:
In an AI feature, a change to a prompt, a tool description, a retrieval setting, a schema or the model version can change behaviour as much as a code change. Most of these changes don’t go through a compiler or a type check, so the eval is the only test that catches regressions. A regression gate is a rule that blocks a change from merging or shipping when the eval says it made things worse.

Tiered suites

TierRuns onContentsTime budget
SmokeEvery pull request touching prompts, tools or context20 to 30 cases, mostly code-graded: schema valid, required tool called, no banned contentUnder 5 minutes
CoreBefore merge to mainThe full golden set with judges, one runUnder 30 minutes
ReleaseBefore deploy, and for every model upgradeCore plus long-tail, long-session and adversarial slices, 3 or more runs per case for pass^kHours is acceptable

Anthropic’s guidance on agent evals separates capability evals, which start with a low pass rate and give the team something to climb, from regression evals, which should sit near 100% and catch backsliding. Cases graduate from the first to the second once the system reliably passes them. Gates belong on regression evals; capability evals inform the roadmap (Lesson 6).

Writing gate rules that survive noise

Outputs are samples, so the same system scores differently run to run. A gate that fires on any drop will be ignored within a month. Rules that hold up:

  • Critical cases are absolute. Any critical-case failure blocks, and on the release tier the case must pass on all k runs.
  • Compare case by case. Count cases that flipped from pass to fail and from fail to pass on identical inputs. Twelve new failures offset by fourteen new passes shows up as +2% and hides twelve regressions someone needs to read.
  • Use a noise threshold. Measure run-to-run spread on an unchanged system, then block only drops larger than that spread on the overall rate or on any slice.
  • Quarantine flaky cases. A case that passes on some runs and fails on others of the same system is telling you about reliability, so track it separately rather than letting it trip the gate at random.

Model upgrades are the big one

A new model version changes behaviour on every case at once, often improving the average while breaking specific slices. Run the release tier, read every flipped case, and check cost and latency guardrails, since newer models can spend more thinking tokens on the same task. Chapter 10 covers shadow runs and rollout.

Gates also need an override path. A product owner can accept a known regression for a larger gain, but the decision is written down with the flipped cases attached. That record is what lets you explain six months later why a behaviour changed.

What changes for you

  • Require that any pull request touching prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, schemas or model versions runs the eval, with results attached to the review.
  • Write gate rules in the eval spec: critical cases, noise threshold, slices that can block, and who can override.
  • Ask for flipped-case lists, not only aggregate deltas, when reviewing a change.

Once error analysis and a golden set exist, the eval becomes the most precise statement of what the product should do. That makes it the natural unit of planning. An eval-driven roadmap expresses quality work as measurable targets on named slices instead of as features.

Feature-style roadmap itemEval-driven version
Improve refund answersRefund slice pass-all rate from 62% to 85%; critical “current policy cited” at 100% pass^3
Support SpanishSpanish slice at parity with English within 5 points, on a 60-case set built from real Spanish tickets
Make the agent more reliablepass^3 on the 40-case booking workflow from 55% to 80%, with cost per task flat
Reduce hallucinationUngrounded-claim rate below 2% on the groundedness judge (sensitivity ≥ 0.9 on 150 labelled cases)

Each target is falsifiable, has a baseline and tells engineering when it is done. It also leaves the method open. The refund target might be met by a retrieval change, a context change, a model change or a new tool, and the team can try the cheapest first (the Chapter 1 ladder).

The weekly eval review

Replace part of the status meeting with a 30-minute eval review. A good agenda:

  1. Trend of the headline pass rate and each roadmap slice, with interval or run-to-run spread shown.
  2. Flipped cases since last week, and the change that caused each.
  3. Five to ten production traces read together, and any new failure modes.
  4. Judge calibration status and golden set changes.
  5. Decisions: which target to attack next, which cases to add, which criteria to retire.

Evals as a bet on future models

Keep a set of aspirational cases: tasks the current system fails that would matter a lot if it could do them. Re-run them on every new model release. When a model starts passing them, you learn about a new capability within days of release, while competitors are still reading launch posts. This is the practical core of building for the model six months out (Chapter 13, Strategy on a moving frontier).

Saturation is a planning signal

When a slice sits near 100% for several weeks, it has become a regression suite. Move it into the gate and stop reporting it as progress. Then add harder cases from recent error analysis, or the roadmap will show success while users meet failures the set no longer covers.

Launch thresholds follow from the autonomy level (Chapter 9, Designing AI experiences). A feature that drafts for a person to review can ship at a lower pass rate than one that acts on its own, because the person catches failures. Write the threshold per autonomy level in the eval spec, and revisit it when you move a feature up the dial.

What changes for you

  • Write quality roadmap items as eval targets with a slice, a baseline, a target and a pass^k requirement where reliability matters.
  • Run a weekly 30-minute eval review with trends, flipped cases and live trace reading.
  • Maintain an aspirational case set and re-run it on every major model release.
  • Tie launch thresholds to autonomy level in the spec.

lab.title: Build a 50-case eval for a live feature
lab.time: about 3 hours for the first build, then 30 minutes a week
lab.intro: This lab produces a working eval in one sitting: a rubric grounded in real failures, 50 cases with a coverage plan, a baseline with honest error bars, and a weekly run you can report on. It is deliberately small. Fifty cases detects large changes; you will grow it later.
steps: Pick the feature and define a pass (10 minutes). Choose one live AI feature with real traffic. Write one sentence that says what a successful output does for the user. Pin the model version and settings you will evaluate.

Read 100 traces (75 minutes). Export 100 recent traces: 70 random and 30 flagged (thumbs down, regenerate, escalation). Open-code each in one line. Then group the notes into 4 to 8 failure modes and count them. Stop early only if the last 20 traces produced no new category.

Write the rubric (20 minutes). Turn the top failure modes into 3 to 6 binary criteria using the rubric template below. Each criterion tests one behaviour, has a concrete pass and fail definition, and names its grader. Mark one or two as critical.

Assemble 50 cases (30 minutes). Take 25 representative cases from the random sample, 15 that target your top failure modes (about 3 to 5 per mode), and 10 edge or adversarial cases (empty or malformed input, contradictions, out-of-scope requests, injection attempts, other languages). Fill in the case sheet with slice tags and the expected behaviour or a reference answer. Check that no slice you care about has fewer than 5 cases.

Hand-grade and wire graders (30 minutes). Grade all 50 outputs yourself against the rubric. Implement code graders where a rule decides. For judge criteria, write one judge prompt per criterion with a pass and a fail example, run it on the 50 cases and compare with your grades. Record agreement, sensitivity on passes and specificity on fails, and note that 50 cases is a starting check; plan to grow labels to 100 or more per judge.

Run the baseline (15 minutes). Run the full eval three times on the pinned system. Record the mean pass-all rate, the spread across runs, per-criterion rates and pass^3 on critical cases. Note the confidence interval: at 50 cases it is roughly ±11 to ±14 points, so treat smaller weekly moves as noise unless the case-level flips explain them.

Schedule the weekly run. Freeze 40 cases as the core and rotate 10 slots for fresh production traces each week, promoting any that reveal a new failure mode into the core (and raising the core size). Run three times weekly and on every change to prompts, tools, retrieval or model. Version the rubric and the case set with each run.

Report the trend. Each week fill in the report template and send a three-sentence summary: the trend, the biggest flip and its cause, and the next target. After four weeks, compare the trend with your main online metric (Lesson 4).

lab.done: A versioned rubric with 3 to 6 binary criteria, each traced to a counted failure mode; 50 slice-tagged cases with your hand grades; code graders for every rule-checkable criterion and judges with measured agreement; a baseline with run-to-run spread; and a weekly run on the calendar producing a one-line trend plus flipped-case list. A good first eval often contradicts at least one belief the team held about the feature.

quiz.q: A team launches an assistant with a dashboard of off-the-shelf helpfulness and coherence scores. Scores are high and stable, but support tickets about wrong answers keep rising. What should the PM do first?
o: Add more generic metrics such as fluency and relevance
Switch to a stronger judge model
Read about 100 recent traces, including flagged ones, and build a failure taxonomy with counts
Run an A/B test of two system prompts
quiz.w: Generic metrics measure what is easy to define rather than how this feature fails. Error analysis surfaces the specific failure modes that the eval should then measure.

quiz.q: On a 50-case eval, a prompt change moves the pass rate from 76% to 80%. The engineer wants to ship it as an improvement. What is the right response?
o: Ship it: four points is a clear gain
Look at case-level flips and run-to-run spread; at 50 cases a four-point move is within noise
Reject it: any change under ten points should be discarded
Re-run once; if it is still 80%, it’s proven
quiz.w: At 50 cases the 95% interval is roughly ±11 to ±14 points. Case-by-case flips and repeated runs show whether the change actually fixed anything.

quiz.q: Your groundedness judge shows 94% accuracy against human labels. About 92% of outputs are grounded. What is the main concern?
o: 94% is too low to use
The judge may be passing nearly everything; check its specificity on the human-failed cases
The judge should use a 1–10 scale instead
Accuracy above 90% means it is calibrated
quiz.w: With imbalanced labels, a judge that passes everything scores about 92% accuracy. Specificity on fails tells you whether it catches the failures you care about.

quiz.q: Offline eval scores rose for three straight releases, but acceptance rate and retries in production haven’t moved. What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Users need time to notice; wait another quarter
The online metrics are wrong; remove them
The golden set no longer reflects production or is saturated; run error analysis on recent traces and update the set
Increase the model’s thinking budget
quiz.w: When offline and online disagree, production is the ground truth. Distribution shift and saturation are the common causes, and fresh error analysis fixes the eval.

quiz.q: Which regression gate rule is most likely to stay useful over months?
o: Block any change where the overall pass rate drops at all
Block only if the judge model’s score falls below 50%
Let engineers decide case by case without a written rule
Block if any critical case fails, or if the overall or any slice drop exceeds measured run-to-run spread; attach flipped cases
quiz.w: Absolute rules on critical cases plus a noise-aware threshold avoid both missed regressions and false alarms that get the gate ignored.

quiz.q: Your agent handles a booking workflow. The roadmap item says “make the agent more reliable”. Which rewrite best fits an eval-driven roadmap?
o: “Raise pass^3 on the 40-case booking set from 55% to 80% with cost per task flat”
“Improve agent reliability significantly this quarter”
“Move to the newest model”
“Reduce user complaints about bookings”
quiz.w: It names a slice, a baseline, a target, a reliability measure and a guardrail, and leaves the method open so the team can try the cheapest fix first.

deliverable.title: Eval spec (replaces the requirements section of the PRD)
deliverable.html:
A one-page definition of “good” that engineering can build and test against. It replaces prose requirements for any AI behaviour. Keep it versioned next to the eval code.

  1. Outcome. One sentence on what a successful output does for the user, and the autonomy level (Chapter 9).
  2. Failure taxonomy. The top failure modes from error analysis, with counts, sample size and date.
  3. Rubric. 3 to 8 binary criteria with pass and fail definitions, grader type for each, and which are critical.
  4. Dataset. Size, composition by source (production, failure-targeted, edge, synthetic), coverage matrix by slice, held-out portion, and refresh rule.
  5. Graders and calibration. For each judge: pinned model and prompt version, sensitivity and specificity on human labels with sample size, and next re-calibration date.
  6. Launch thresholds. Pass-all rate per slice, pass^k on critical cases, and the cost and latency guardrails.
  7. Regression gate. Which suite runs on which change, the noise threshold, blocking slices, and who may override and how it is recorded.
  8. Online metrics. The primary metric, two or three guardrails, and the online judge sampling rate.
  9. Ownership and cadence. Quality owner, weekly review slot, and trace-reading quota.

If a requirement can’t be written as a rubric item with a grader, it isn’t yet precise enough to build.
